mcq.q: Which feature is the best fit for AI with little risk?
options: Drafting replies that agents edit before sending
Calculating tax owed from fixed rules
mcq.why: Errors are cheap and a person checks quickly.

mcq.q: If simple rules fully capture a task, the best choice is…
options: Use AI with a person reviewing
mcq.why: Deterministic code is cheaper, testable and exact (7.7).

mcq.q: Drafts cut reply time from 6 to 2 minutes for 1,000 replies a day. Time saved per day is about…
mcq.why: 4 minutes × 1,000 = 4,000 minutes ≈ 67 hours.

mcq.q: Which level of automation suits a reversible, rarely wrong action?
mcq.why: Reversible actions with low error rates can act, if undo is easy.
distractors: Too heavy for a low-risk action.

mcq.q: 1% of 10,000 daily refunds are wrong and each costs 2,000 rupees to recover. The daily cost is…
A team wants an assistant that approves refunds alone after a good pilot on easy cases. The main concern is…
options: High error cost and an unrepresentative pilot
Refunds cannot be drafted by an AI model
The model is too slow for refund work
mcq.why: Easy-case pilots overstate accuracy; errors are costly.

mcq.q: Two numbers decide the right level of automation most directly:
options: The price per token and the latency
The model size and the context length
The number of users and their ages
The cost of an error and the cost of checking
mcq.why: Cheap errors and cheap checks allow more automation.

mcq.q: A refund feature combines reading the message, computing the amount and approving. A good split is…
options: Code reads, AI computes and AI approves
People do all three of the steps by hand
AI reads, code computes, people approve large ones
AI does all three steps entirely on its own
mcq.why: Each part goes to what does it best and safest.

mcq.q: Drafts are wrong 10% of the time and each wrong draft costs 4 extra minutes. For 1,000 drafts, the extra time is…
Why start at a lower automation level and raise it later?
options: Evidence from use justifies each step up
Higher levels are always cheaper later
mcq.why: Measured performance earns more autonomy.

mcq.q: Why is a citation to a document that does not support the claim dangerous?
options: It looks verified when it is not
It breaks the prompt cache for others
It uses too many tokens per answer
It slows down the whole answer
mcq.why: Users trust cited sentences more; a false citation misleads.

mcq.q: Answers labelled "high" are right 93% of the time on held-out data. This means the labels are…
mcq.why: A label that matches observed accuracy can be trusted.
distractors: They hold on the measured data.

mcq.q: An answer has a sentence with no supporting passage. The safest display is to…
options: Show it with a citation anyway
Hide all citations in the answer
Remove it or mark it as unverified
mcq.why: Unsupported claims should not look supported.

mcq.q: Why say "likely" or "please check this" rather than "0.73"?
options: Plain words are easier to act on
mcq.why: People interpret words more consistently than raw scores.

mcq.q: 40% of answers carry a warning. The likely effect is…
mcq.why: Too many warnings cause warning blindness.

mcq.q: Labels "high" were right only 70% of the time. How many users in 10 are misled by "high"?
mcq.why: 30% wrong = 3 in 10.
distractors: That is how many are right.

mcq.q: A store answer mixes a listed specification and a reviewer’s opinion. The interface should…
options: Label the opinion as from reviews
Cite the review as the listing
mcq.why: Users need to know the source type.

mcq.q: "I couldn’t find this in the policies" is…
options: A failure to hide from users
A sign the index is empty
mcq.why: Abstaining beats guessing (9.6).

mcq.q: A fee is quoted from a fare rule checked 3 days ago. The display should add…
options: A bigger font for the fee
mcq.why: Time-sensitive facts need their check time.

mcq.q: On 1,000 answers, those scored 0.6–0.85 are right 78% of the time. Of 200 such answers, about how many are wrong?

interview.q: How should an AI interface show uncertainty?
interview.followUp: When would you show a number?

interview.q: Why must confidence labels be calibrated?
What makes a citation trustworthy?
interview.followUp: How do you check support at scale?

interview.q: Users trust wrong answers because they look confident. What do you change?
interview.followUp: How do you measure the change?

interview.q: How do you avoid warning blindness?
interview.followUp: How do you decide which answers get a warning?

interview.q: How would you display prices and fees that change often?
interview.followUp: What if the price changed during the chat?

interview.q: Design the answer display for a policy assistant used by 8,000 staff.
Plan how you would test whether users trust answers appropriately.

mcq.q: Perceived latency depends most on…
options: Time to the first sign of progress
The size of the context window
mcq.why: Early feedback changes how long a wait feels.
distractors: Total time matters less than first feedback.

mcq.q: The full answer takes 9 seconds and the first token comes at 0.8. Streaming shows something about how many times sooner?
Which wait suits running in the background with a notification?
mcq.why: Nobody watches a screen for minutes.

mcq.q: Why not stream a structured action before it is validated?
options: Actions cannot be streamed to users at all
Users may see a change that never happens
It doubles the token cost of each action
Streaming is much slower for JSON output
mcq.why: Validate actions first; stream prose.
distractors: They can be, but should not be.

mcq.q: An agent has 6 steps of 4 seconds. Showing each finished step keeps the longest silent gap at…
mcq.why: Each step ends with visible progress.

mcq.q: A rebooking agent shows only a spinner and users refresh and start second requests. The best fix is…
options: Show finished steps as the agent works
Hide the request until it finishes
mcq.why: Visible progress stops users giving up or retrying.

mcq.q: An acknowledgement within 0.3 seconds mainly tells the user…
options: The model is the largest one available
The request was answered from the cache
The request was received and work has started
The final answer is going to be correct
mcq.why: Instant acknowledgement prevents doubt and repeats.

mcq.q: During a sale the first token slows from 0.8 to 3 seconds. A cheap mitigation in the interface is…
options: Ask users to come back later
Show a short status within 300 ms
mcq.why: Early status keeps people waiting while tokens arrive.

mcq.q: A report takes 2 minutes. Holding the chat open until it finishes risks…
mcq.why: Long synchronous waits fail; move them to the background (15.4).

mcq.q: Which balance figure should a bank assistant stream?
options: The figure from the last session
Only figures confirmed by the core system
mcq.why: Unconfirmed money figures mislead.

interview.q: How do you design the waiting experience of an AI feature?
What are the risks of streaming?
Why does time to first feedback matter more than total time?
Users refresh during long agent tasks, creating duplicates. What do you do?
How do you keep the interface responsive when the model slows at peak?
interview.followUp: Where is the line before you degrade?

interview.q: Which tasks should move to the background?
interview.followUp: How does the user get the result?

interview.q: Design the interface for an agent that takes 20–60 seconds.
interview.followUp: What if a step fails half-way?

interview.q: Plan latency targets for the interface and back end together.

mcq.q: In draft, review, commit, what is executed?
options: The first draft the AI produced
Only the version the person approved
The last version the AI wrote
Any version saved during the session
mcq.why: The approved version is the one that runs (11.7).
distractors: May differ from what was approved.

mcq.q: Which action can an undo window really reverse?
options: Saving a draft or moving a label
mcq.why: Only reversible actions can be undone.

mcq.q: Reviewers see 6 of 9 mistakes and catch 80% of those. About how many are caught?
Reviewers approve 99% of drafts unchanged. This most likely shows…
options: The review step can be removed
mcq.why: Near-zero edit rates signal inattentive review (13.2).

mcq.q: A diff view is most useful for…
options: Edits to existing records or documents
Generating a brand-new image from text
Showing a loading spinner while waiting
mcq.why: It shows exactly what will change.

mcq.q: An amount changes after approval. The right rule is…
options: Keep the old approval since it was close
A new approval of the exact action
Let the agent decide if it matters
mcq.why: Approvals apply to one immutable version.

mcq.q: Undo catches half of the 4 mistakes that slip past review. How many remain for reconciliation?
A travel change should be shown before confirmation as…
options: Only the fare difference, as a number
The new itinerary and total cost beside the old
Only the new flight number and time
mcq.why: People need the full consequence to decide.

mcq.q: Why are reviewers’ edits valuable beyond catching errors?
options: They are training and evaluation data
They make the model respond faster
They remove the need for any audit
They reduce the token cost of drafts
mcq.why: Edits show the preferred output (18.6).

mcq.q: 150 actions, 6% wrong. How many mistakes enter the review and undo layers?

interview.q: Explain the draft, review, commit pattern.
When is undo enough and when is review needed?
How do you design a review screen that prevents rubber-stamping?
Reviewers miss wrong amounts in a busy queue. What do you change?
interview.followUp: How would you test the change?

interview.q: How do you handle mistakes that undo cannot reverse?
How do you use reviewer edits?
interview.followUp: What do you do about privacy?

interview.q: Design the human-control layer for an agent that changes bookings.
interview.followUp: What happens when confirmation times out?

interview.q: Plan review capacity for a feature with 10,000 proposed actions a day.

mcq.q: Why is the thumbs-down share not the true rate of bad answers?
options: Each thumb click is counted twice
Unhappy users click more than happy ones
Thumbs buttons are not stored anywhere
Only expert users are able to click
mcq.why: Feedback is self-selected and biased.

mcq.q: Of 10,000 sessions, 1,200 are bad; 8% of those click down and 2% of 8,800 good ones click up. The thumbs-down share is about…
Which signal is collected for every session, not only clickers?
mcq.why: Behavioural signals come from everyone (17.4).

mcq.q: Thumbs-down falls from 1.0% to 0.9% with 20,000 sessions each. The right conclusion is…
options: The new prompt is clearly worse
The new prompt is clearly better
mcq.why: Rare events need far more sessions to detect small changes (8.7).

mcq.q: Reason chips after a thumbs down mainly…
mcq.why: Reasons point to the failure type.
distractors: They add a step, so fewer.

mcq.q: To validate a quick satisfaction click, join it with…
options: Later outcomes such as support calls
The length of the answer in tokens
The time of day the chat happened
mcq.why: Outcomes confirm whether the proxy tracks reality (17.7).

mcq.q: A prompt change cuts the draft edit rate from 34% to 19%. Compared with thumbs, this signal is…
mcq.why: Every draft yields an edit rate; it measures the work saved.

mcq.q: Feedback must be stored with…
options: The trace id, prompt and model versions
Nothing else at all, for privacy
Only the text of the answer
mcq.why: Links let you reproduce and fix the case.

mcq.q: A thumbs-down rate of 1% falling by a fifth needs about 35,000 sessions per version. With 5,000 sessions a day, a test takes about…
mcq.why: 70,000 sessions ÷ 5,000 = 14 days.

mcq.q: What should happen after the weekly feedback review?
options: Findings become eval cases and fixes
mcq.why: Closing the loop is the point (17.9).

mcq.q: Why is "Ask me anything" a weak onboarding message?
options: It is too short for users to read
It reveals the name of the model
It invites questions the system cannot answer
It uses too many tokens in each prompt
mcq.why: Specific examples set honest expectations.

mcq.q: Of 1,000 conversations, 20% fail and a generic error gives no next step. How many dead ends?
The booking system is down. The best message is…
options: Saved; we will retry and notify you
mcq.why: It explains and gives a next step.

mcq.q: For a low-confidence answer, a good pattern is…
options: Hide the answer from the user completely
Ask the user to rephrase again and again
Show the answer as if it were certain
Show what was found with sources and suggest checking
mcq.why: Partial help with honesty beats nothing.

mcq.q: With designed next steps, half of 200 failing users recover. How many more users succeed?
Why include a way to reach a person in every failure message?
options: Some problems need a human decision
mcq.why: A handover prevents loops and dead ends.

mcq.q: How should failure messages be tested?
options: Read the code that prints each message
Wait for real outages to happen in production
Ask the model to describe its own messages
Inject each failure and look at what users see
mcq.why: Fault injection shows the real experience.

mcq.q: During a disruption, the assistant’s opening message should…
options: Ask the traveller for a rating before anything else
List every feature the app offers today
Say which flights are affected and what it can do
Repeat the usual greeting as on a normal day
mcq.why: Context and capabilities set expectations at the worst moment.

mcq.q: A timeout message offers "keep waiting or get it by email". This is an example of…
options: A failure hidden from the user
A designed failure with a next step
mcq.why: It turns a failure into a choice.

mcq.q: Failure types are 7% low confidence, 5% out of scope, 4% tool failure, 4% timeout. Which share needs a handover or retry message?
